summary: Reviewed run_r20_gpu.py, run_r20_pod.py, attach_pod.py and stop_watcher.py plus the live local logs/status files (no pod or RunPod API contact). Current state as of 15:18 UTC 09-04: three runners alive (setsid, ppid 1): t1 -> oxgcuwlleea1fd (A100 SXM, all-ones, seed 3971886063, 8.76e8 a0/s), t2 -> 3r52zyawqj9jd7 (A100 PCIe, all-ones, seed 1138247750, 8.25e8 a0/s), dev -> b69rcro3uqlki1 (the re-used a100a pod, hand-started solver, hedge target d962ca30..., 7.10e8 a0/s); all three polled RUNNING; stop_watcher alive (pid 788617) and no r20*HIT.txt or GLOBAL_STOP present. The earlier H100 (n2zom46pxzmcgg) and a100b (9sqc6t0c47dfe9) pods were confirmed deleted (HTTP 204 then 404). Bounded-billing verdict: as long as the runner processes stay alive and one DELETE call succeeds, every pod is bounded at 61 h; there is no unbounded path in normal operation. The real gaps are (1) a single un-retried DELETE with no registry/reaper if a runner dies by SIGKILL/reboot/OOM, (2) the only local copies of a hit live in /tmp (tmpfiles: removed at boot, 30-day age) and the pod is deleted even when the HIT.txt scp fails, (3) attach_pod.py's fetch() does not catch scp TimeoutExpired, so a 300 s stall deletes the hedge pod and can destroy an unfetched hit, (4) ssh failure is treated as "keep waiting" up to 61 h (t1 already logged one <ssh failed> at 15:12:40), (5) GLOBAL_STOP is target-blind: a hedge hit stops the two all-ones pods, (6) the 60/61 h caps are ~13x the mean; P(no hit in 24 h) < 1%, so anything beyond ~24 h is bug-hunting money (max exposure $291 vs $115), (7) dev runs 19% slower than the identical-SKU t1 pod, consistent with a leftover process on the reused pod. Cost arithmetic checks: 3 x 1.59 = 4.77 $/h; 4.77/0.216 = $22.1 and 1/0.216 = 4.63 h are correct, but 0.216/h assumes 0.072/pod-h (9.2e8 a0/s); measured rates from the status files give 0.0664+0.0649+0.0559 = 0.187/h -> mean 5.3 h -> ~$25.5 plus ~$1 of boot/shutdown latency, i.e. $26-27 to the first hit on EITHER target (an all-ones-only hit at 0.131/h averages 7.6 h). Earlier fleet: H100 19.69 h x $3.49 = $68.70, a100a 8.64 h x 1.59 = $13.74, a100b 8.86 h x 1.59 = $14.08, total $96.5 for 0.690+0.173+0.176 = 1.038 expected preimages ($93/expected preimage vs ~$24 with the Triton kernel), so "~$95 for 1.03" is right and stopping the old fleet was correct. Concrete hardening: (a) write a pods registry (tag, pod_id, created_at, cap) at creation and run a cron reaper that GETs /pods and deletes any sha20-* pod whose runner PID is dead or age > cap; retry DELETE with backoff until GET returns 404 and alert if not; (b) never delete a pod while found=True unless the local HIT file exists and re-verifies (independent SHA-256), retry scp, else leave the pod up ($1.59/h) and alert; also `cat HIT.txt` over ssh into the runner log and copy hits to the repo experiments dir, not /tmp; (c) wrap attach_pod fetch() in try/except TimeoutExpired; (d) count consecutive ssh failures, after 6 GET the pod, re-resolve ip/port, and after 1 h delete+alert; (e) make GLOBAL_STOP per-target (or an explicit policy) and have the watcher only honour hit files newer than its start; refuse to launch a runner if GLOBAL_STOP exists; (f) cut caps to 24 h; (g) add a push/email in the watcher on hit; (h) check nvidia-smi on the dev pod for a second solver process; (i) keep the RunPod prepaid balance modest as the last-ditch hard cap.

findings.claim: Runner death without a Python exception (SIGKILL, OOM, host reboot, or the deliberate kill -9 used to keep pod b69rcro3uqlki1 alive) leaves the pod billed indefinitely: the pod ID exists only in a log line in /tmp, there is no registry and no reaper, and the finally-block DELETE is a single un-retried call whose failure (status 0 on a network error, 429/5xx) is merely logged.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py lines 144-149 and attach_pod.py lines 78-81: one api('DELETE') then an informational GET; api() returns 0 on any exception (lines 46-49 / 35-36). r20_a100a_run.log ends at 14:41:19 with RUNNING and no delete line, i.e. that runner died without its finally running; the pod survived and was re-attached by hand at 15:11:04. /tmp is 'D /tmp 1777 root root 30d' (removed at boot).
findings.fix: At create time append {tag,pod_id,created_at,cap_h,runner_pid} to a durable registry (e.g. ~/sha/pods.json). Add reap_pods.py on a 15-min cron: GET /pods, and for every pod named sha20-* whose registry runner PID is not alive or whose age exceeds cap, DELETE with retries (5 tries, exponential backoff) until GET returns 404, and log/alert otherwise. Make the runners' finally use the same retry-until-404 helper.

findings.claim: A verified hit can be lost: the pod is deleted even when the scp of HIT.txt fails (return codes ignored, no local-existence check), and the only local copies (r20_*_HIT.txt, runner log) live in /tmp which is wiped at boot.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py lines 141-142 loop scp over four files ignoring rc, then finally deletes at line 145; attach_pod.py lines 75-79 same. HIT.txt on the pod is on container disk (volumeInGb 0, line 78) so nothing survives deletion. The solver writes HIT.txt only after CPU rebuild() verification (submask_triton.py lines 360-379), so a lost HIT.txt is a lost verified preimage.
findings.fix: Before DELETE, if found: (1) retry scp of HIT.txt up to 10 times, (2) `ssh ... cat HIT.txt` and write the words into the runner log, (3) require the local file to exist, be non-empty and re-verify with an independent SHA-256 (reviewers/independent_audit_sha.py) before deleting; otherwise leave the pod running ($1.59/h) and alert. Copy hits immediately to /home/administrator/sha/publish/experiments/... rather than /tmp. Optionally give pods volumeInGb=5 at /workspace so a stop (not delete) preserves HIT.txt.

findings.claim: attach_pod.py fetch() does not catch subprocess.TimeoutExpired: a 300 s scp stall (status.json each poll, or HIT.txt right after a hit) raises out of main(), the finally DELETEs the hedge pod, and if the stall was on the HIT.txt fetch the hit is destroyed with the pod.
findings.evidence: attach_pod.py lines 49-52: subprocess.run(..., timeout=300) with no try/except, called at lines 66, 70 and 76 inside the try whose finally is DELETE (line 79). By contrast run_r20_pod.py's scp() catches TimeoutExpired (lines 70-72).
findings.fix: Wrap fetch() in try/except subprocess.TimeoutExpired returning a failed CompletedProcess, and apply the found/HIT-exists guard above before DELETE.

findings.claim: Persistent ssh failure (pod restarted by RunPod with a new port, IP change, home network outage) is treated as 'keep waiting': the runner loops for the full 61 h wall cap paying $1.59/h for a pod it can no longer see, and any hit on it is unrecoverable at cap time because the final scp fails too.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py line 132: on rc != 0 lines = ['<ssh failed>'] and the loop only breaks on found/EXITED/GLOBAL_STOP/WALL_CAP. r20_t1_run.log already shows '[09-04 15:12:40] t=0.27h | <ssh failed>' (transient, recovered at 15:17:42).
findings.fix: Count consecutive failures; after 6 (30 min) GET /pods/{id} and re-resolve publicIp/portMappings['22'] (pods can be re-scheduled); after 12 (1 h) with the pod still unreachable, delete it via the retry helper and alert. Log a WARN with the failure count so a human notices.

findings.claim: The 60 h solver / 61 h runner caps are ~13x the mean time-to-hit; they bound the loss but at $291 (3 x 61 x 1.59) plus $14 already spent on the reused dev pod, when a 24 h cap would already have P(no hit) < 1% and cap exposure at $115. A no-hit run beyond ~20 h is far more likely a kernel/target bug than bad luck, and the Triton production path records no C3 counters to diagnose it in flight.
findings.evidence: P(no hit by 60 h) = exp(-0.216*60) = 2.3e-6; by 24 h 0.006; by 20 h 0.013. submask_triton.py status.json (lines 370-374) has no c3_lowk_zero counters unlike gpu_submask.py; run_r20_pod.py line 20/22 HOURS=60, WALL_CAP=61 h; attach_pod.py default 61 h measured from attach time (15:11) not pod creation (06:02), so dev's total life could reach ~70 h ($111).
findings.fix: Relaunch policy: --hours 24 and WALL_CAP 25 h; add a soft alarm in the runner when elapsed*rate > 3 expected preimages without a hit (push/email); for attach_pod pass the remaining budget explicitly, computed from pod creation time.

findings.claim: GLOBAL_STOP is target-blind and never cleared: a hit on the hedge pod (random digest d962ca30...) stops the two all-ones pods, forfeiting the priority-relevant target and forcing a relaunch; conversely a stale r20*HIT.txt or leftover r20_GLOBAL_STOP would stop any future fleet at its first poll after paying for creation. The watcher is also one-shot (breaks after the first hit) and its pgrep pattern 'python3 run_r20_gpu.py' now matches nothing since the H100 runner finished at 14:44:43.
findings.evidence: stop_watcher.py lines 15-25 (glob r20*HIT.txt, write GLOBAL_STOP, pgrep, break); run_r20_pod.py line 137 and attach_pod.py line 71 honour GLOBAL_STOP unconditionally; ps shows only run_r20_pod.py t1/t2 and attach_pod.py dev running. Currently no HIT/STOP files exist (verified).
findings.fix: Name hit and stop files per target (r20_<hash8>_GLOBAL_STOP) or decide explicitly that any 20-round preimage ends the campaign; have the watcher ignore hit files older than its own start and loop forever; make runners refuse to start when a matching GLOBAL_STOP exists; drop the dead pgrep branch.

findings.claim: Two-pods-hit-within-one-poll race is benign for hits but costs up to ~11 min of extra billing: after a hit at T, that runner deletes at <= T+5 min, the watcher flags at <= T+6 min, the other two runners see it at <= T+11 min; every runner still runs the post-loop scp of HIT.txt regardless of why it broke, so a second hit is copied, not lost.
findings.evidence: Timing from POLL=300 (run_r20_pod.py line 23, attach_pod.py line 61) and the watcher's 60 s sleep; post-loop copy at run_r20_pod.py lines 141-142 and attach_pod.py 75-76 runs after any break. Worst-case extra cost 2 x 11 min x $1.59/h = $0.58.
findings.fix: Acceptable as is; optionally lower POLL to 120 s (ssh load is trivial).

findings.claim: The hand-restarted solvers on t1/t2 (runners were launched without a target, status files now show target ffff... with new seeds) and the reused dev pod leave no local record of the actual --hours or of whether the previous solver was killed; dev's steady-state rate 7.10e8 a0/s is 19% below t1's 8.76e8 on the same A100-SXM4-80GB SKU, consistent with a leftover gpu_submask.py process sharing the GPU (which would also write to the same run.log/status.json/HIT.txt).
findings.evidence: ps: 'run_r20_pod.py t1 ... 60' with no 4th argument (TARGET None, line 21); r20_t1_run.log shows the ctx counter reset between 15:02 (ctx 21, 9.4e10) and 15:07 (ctx 3, 1.7e10); r20_dev_status.json a0_per_s 7.107e8 vs r20_t1_status.json 8.45e8 (poll line 8.76e8); r20_a100a_run.log last poll at 14:41 showed the old solver RUNNING at 2.54e8 a0/s with no shutdown recorded.
findings.fix: On the dev pod (user action, not this reviewer): `nvidia-smi; pgrep -af submask` and kill any gpu_submask.py survivor; record the exact hand-start command lines (target, seed, --hours) in the runner logs. Future runs: pass the target as argv[4] so the runner header, status and pod agree.

findings.claim: create_pod() can orphan a pod: if the POST times out (api returns status 0) after RunPod created the pod, the loop tries the next GPU type and may create a second pod; the first is never tracked or deleted.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py lines 76-86: any non-2xx/no-id response falls through to the next candidate; api() maps timeouts to (0, error). Both A100 runners already hit an HTTP 500 on the first candidate and created on the second.
findings.fix: Use a unique name per attempt (sha20-<tag>-<epoch>) and, after any ambiguous response, GET /pods and delete any pod with that name before retrying; the cron reaper above also covers this.

findings.claim: Nobody is notified on a hit or on a runner failure; a verified preimage would sit as 'finished: found=True' in a /tmp log until someone looks, and a failed DELETE is a single log line.
findings.evidence: All alerting is log() to files in the scratchpad (run_r20_pod.py line 30-34, stop_watcher.py line 11-12); no push, email or repo write.
findings.fix: Have the watcher (and the reaper) send a push notification / email on hit, on any DELETE that does not reach 404, and on a runner whose log has not advanced in 15 min.

findings.claim: Cost arithmetic is consistent: 3 x $1.59 = $4.77/h, 1/0.216 = 4.63 h, $22.1 expected; with measured per-pod rates (0.0664, 0.0649, 0.0559/h from the status files, sum 0.187/h) the mean is 5.3 h and ~$26-27 including boot/shutdown latency, and that is the cost to the first hit on EITHER target (all-ones alone: 0.131/h, mean 7.6 h). Earlier fleet: $68.70 (H100 19.69 h @ $3.49) + $13.74 + $14.08 = $96.5 for 1.038 expected preimages, so '~$95 for 1.03' is right; the old fleet cost $93 per expected preimage vs ~$24 now, so abandoning it (memoryless search) was correct.
findings.evidence: Timestamps and cost/h from r20_gpu_run.log, r20_a100a_run.log, r20_a100b_run.log; expected_preimages from r20_status.json (0.6896), r20_a100a_status.json (0.1725), r20_a100b_status.json (0.1755); new-fleet rates from r20_t1/t2/dev_status.json.
findings.fix: Quote ~$25-27 and 'first hit on either target' rather than $22; note the H100 hourly rate was $3.49, not the A100 rate.

findings.claim: Signal handling is adequate for the current launch mode: all three runners are setsid'ed with ppid 1, SIGTERM/SIGHUP (run_r20_pod.py) or SIGTERM (attach_pod.py, via the generator .throw trick) raise SystemExit so the finally deletes the pod; SIGINT does too. Only SIGKILL and a signal arriving during the finally itself bypass deletion. Note the inverse trap: SIGTERM to a run_r20_pod.py runner deletes its pod, so detaching a runner while keeping the pod requires kill -9, which is exactly what created the untracked pod earlier today.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py lines 152-158, attach_pod.py lines 84-87; ps shows sid == pid for all three runners.
findings.fix: Add a SIGUSR1 handler meaning 'detach without deleting' (write the registry entry and exit) so kill -9 is never needed; keep SIGTERM = delete.

summary: The science behind the new work holds up under the checks I could run locally: the planted-preimage pipeline test reproduces deterministically (10 found / 6 missing-root / 0 failures, seed 2026), and I independently re-verified all 10 recovered 20-round preimages with the stdlib verifier (verify_r19.py --rounds 20: 10/10 OK; words saved at scratchpad/_plant_print.log). The measured Triton production rate (402.8k submask candidates per 2^32 a0 on t1) matches theory, and the memory's binomial-halving C3 statistic (2,092 of 4,225) recomputes exactly from the committed h100_status.json. What is NOT in order is the archival and operational state that a referee or a future you would need: (1) every .log in the snapshot is excluded by .gitignore (`*.log`) so the "committed snapshot" contains no logs at all; (2) the MANIFEST is stale (six files changed after it was written, submask_triton.py untracked, final old-fleet statuses uncommitted); (3) the runners can lose the first-ever 20-round hit: the pod's HIT.txt is fetched only at the end without checking the copy succeeded before the pod is deleted, the poll captures only `tail -n 1 run.log` (which after a hit is "DONE"), and the fetched pod log overwrites the local runner log (same filename); none of the three old-fleet pods' own logs were retrieved; (4) the fleet's provenance is partly unrecorded: t1/t2 were started on random targets and hand-restarted on the all-ones digest (~15:06), the a100a runner was SIGKILLed and its pod re-used as "dev" with a hand-started solver whose command/seed are not on disk; (5) the live Triton kernel collects no C3 statistics, so the ~10^9 candidates now being generated add nothing to the only empirical check of the 2^-32 assumption, and C3 uniformity has never been measured for the all-ones target at all; (6) the Triton --verify (8/8, 4/4) and --bench (3.59x) results exist only in a commit message; the kernel's 27 root-combination paths have been checked against the reference only at the level of aggregate counts. Plus several smaller items: plant_r20.py prints a wrong expected findability (0.40; correct is 0.896^3 = 0.72, I measured 0.899 per lookup), the memory's "3 roots ~78%" should be ~93%, the per-A100 rate 0.0719/h in memory and commit message is 8-10% above the production statuses (0.066/0.065), quantized_table.py and its results are not in the repo, README/requirements do not mention the new scripts or triton, and the audit-accepted --measure/--v fix is still pending.

findings.claim: The 'committed snapshot' contains no logs: every experiments/submask_2026-09-03/logs/*.log and gpu_run_snapshot/*_runner.log is excluded by .gitignore (`*.log`), although MANIFEST.txt lists them with sha256 and the memory file says 'SNAPSHOT COMMITTED (scripts, logs, ...)'.
findings.evidence: `git ls-files experiments/` lists only logs/c3_deep.txt and logs/smoke20_status.json from logs/, and only the three *_status.json from gpu_run_snapshot/; `git status --ignored` marks all 15 .log files `!!`. /home/administrator/sha/publish/.gitignore line 11: `*.log`. The c3_scaling.log, c3_uniformity.log, r19_big.log, r19_scale.log, smoke19_*.log, multiroot_build.log that back the 2^15.26, C3-uniformity and 2-root measurements exist only on this disk.
findings.fix: Add `!experiments/**/*.log` after the `*.log` line in .gitignore (or `git add -f experiments/submask_2026-09-03/logs/*.log experiments/submask_2026-09-03/gpu_run_snapshot/*.log`), commit, and re-verify with `git ls-files experiments/ | grep -c '\.log$'` (expect 18).

findings.claim: MANIFEST.txt is stale and the final state of the old fleet is uncommitted: six listed files no longer match their hashes, scripts/submask_triton.py is untracked and unlisted, and the header still describes the PyTorch (gpu_submask.py) launch commands although the running fleet uses submask_triton.py.
findings.evidence: sha256 recomputation: a100a_runner.log (manifest 12925 B, now 25063 B), a100b_runner.log, and all three *_status.json differ; `git status` shows the three status.json as `M` (final values: H100 0.690, a100a 0.173, a100b 0.172 expected preimages, contexts 7351/1839/1836, 0 hits) and scripts/submask_triton.py as `??`. The MANIFEST header line 5 names run_r20_gpu.py / gpu_submask.py only; scratchpad/run_r20_pod.py (15:05) differs from scripts/run_r20_pod.py (4th arg = target hex, uploads and launches submask_triton.py); attach_pod.py is not in the snapshot.
findings.fix: Copy the current run_r20_pod.py and attach_pod.py into scripts/, commit the final *_status.json, regenerate MANIFEST.txt with `sha256sum` over gpu_run_snapshot/* scripts/* logs/* reviewers/*, and add a line stating that the old fleet (H100 n2zom46pxzmcgg, A100 9sqc6t0c47dfe9, A100 b69rcro3uqlki1) was terminated 2026-09-04 14:44-14:54 after 1.03 expected preimages, 0 hits.

findings.claim: The runners can lose the first 20-round hit: HIT.txt is fetched only after the poll loop exits, the scp result is never checked, and the `finally` block deletes the pod regardless; the periodic poll captures only `tail -n 1 run.log`, which after a hit reads 'DONE' or 'stopping on verified hit', not the words; and the end-of-run fetch writes the pod's run.log to r20_<TAG>_run.log, the same path as the runner's own log.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/run_r20_pod.py line 14 `LOG = ... f"r20_{TAG}_run.log"` vs line 142 `scp(... f"/workspace/r20/{f}", os.path.join(S, f"r20_{TAG}_" + f))` for f in (run.log, ...); lines 141-146 fetch then DELETE with no check. attach_pod.py lines 75-79 identical pattern. Evidence it fails in practice: no r20_stdout.log, r20_a100b_stdout.log or pod-side run.log exists locally for any of the three old pods; r20_a100b_run.log and r20_gpu_run.log show the DELETE lines without a preceding 'finished:' line (loop exited via SIGTERM/SystemExit, fetch skipped); r20_t1_run.log already logged one '<ssh failed>' poll at 15:12.
findings.fix: In the poll command add `cat HIT.txt 2>/dev/null` so the words land in the local runner log the moment they exist; on detecting HIT.txt fetch it immediately, check `os.path.exists(local)` and run `python3 code/verify_r19.py --rounds 20 --words ... --hash ...` before allowing the DELETE (retry the fetch on failure; never delete a pod holding an unfetched HIT.txt); rename the fetched pod log to r20_<TAG>_pod_run.log. The two running runners execute the old code, so apply this to attach_pod.py/run_r20_pod.py for the next launch and, for the live pods, rely on the fact that HIT.txt also appears in status.json['hits'] which IS fetched every 5 minutes.

findings.claim: The live fleet's provenance is only partly on disk: t1 and t2 were launched on random targets and their solvers were restarted by hand on the all-ones digest around 15:06; the a100a runner was killed without its `finally` and its pod b69rcro3uqlki1 was re-used as 'dev' with a hand-started solver whose command line, seed, --hours and target are recorded nowhere locally.
findings.evidence: run_r20_pod.py processes 846611/846623 have no 4th argument (TARGET=None => random target); r20_t1_run.log: 'ctx 21' at 15:02 then 'ctx 3' at 15:07 (counter reset); r20_t2_run.log 15:06 last line is the solver header 'TRITON R=20 ... target=ffff...' (run.log re-opened in append mode). r20_a100a_run.log ends 14:41:19 with no delete line; its pod id b69rcro3uqlki1 / 154.54.102.45:13524 equals the 'dev' pod in attach_dev.stdout. r20_dev_status.json does not exist yet; memory line 1287 says dev target d962ca30... 'solver started by hand'.
findings.fix: Write experiments/submask_2026-09-03/FLEET.txt now (pod id, GPU, kernel, exact solver command, seed, target, start/restart/stop timestamps, $/h) for all six pods; at the next dev poll confirm r20_dev_status.json carries the seed and target and copy it into the snapshot; when the pods finish, fetch /workspace/r20/run.log which (append mode) contains both the random-target prefix and the all-ones run.

findings.claim: The production Triton kernel records no C3 statistics (no c3_lowk_zero, no `c3`, no `sol`), so the ~1.2e9 candidates/hour the fleet now produces contribute nothing to the only empirical check of the P(C3=0)=2^-32 assumption behind 2^47.3; and C3 uniformity has never been measured for the all-ones target that two of three pods are attacking (all prior C3 data — 68k, 2.14M, 2.3e9+2x0.74e9 candidates — are for random-message digests).
findings.evidence: code/submask_triton.py sweep() lines 138-149 count only `sub` and post-C3 hits; production() line 370 status has no c3_lowk_zero key (compare gpu_submask.py lines 182-183, 274). r20_t1_status.json / r20_t2_status.json: keys R, roots, seed, target, contexts, elapsed_s, a0_per_s, expected_preimages, kernel, a0, sub, ver, hits. The nested-halving statistic quoted in memory (2,092/4,225, z=-0.63) is not implemented in any script (grep for Binomial/halving/Bonferroni hits only reviewers/pq_proof.py).
findings.fix: Add per-bit-depth counters to the kernel: after `hit = m3 & (Maj==A3)` compute c3 = _s0(W4)+W3-K3p and `tl.atomic_add(k_ptr+k, tl.sum((hit & ((c3 & ((1<<k)-1))==0)).to(int32)))` for k=0..28 (only ~400k lanes per context reach this, negligible cost); write scripts/c3_halving.py that reads any status.json and prints per-step Binomial(n_k,1/2) z-scores plus the aggregate. Until then, measure the all-ones target on CPU: `scratchpad/venv/bin/python code/gpu_submask.py --rounds 20 --roots 2 --device cpu --smoke --hash ffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff --a0 268435456 --contexts 4 --out <dir>` (about 2^28 a0 at 4e5 a0/s per context, ~25k candidates, uniform to ~10 bits).

findings.claim: The Triton kernel's correctness evidence is not preserved and is thin: the '8/8 and 4/4 planted, 9.30e8 vs 2.60e8' figures exist only in commit df15d89's message and the memory file (the pod's stdout was never fetched), and the kernel's 27 root-combination code paths have been compared with gpu_submask.py only through aggregate counts (verified-hit count per planted window; 403,413 vs 402,970 submask candidates per 2^32) — a path that drops or duplicates hits at the 0.1% level would be invisible.
findings.evidence: `grep -l 'VERIFY PASS\|speedup'` over the scratchpad and experiments finds no log; `git show --stat df15d89` adds only code/submask_triton.py. submask_triton.py --verify (lines 284-306) compares `ver == st['ver']` on 8192-a0 windows with default 12 plants; the kernel stores only post-C3 a0 (line 149), so pre-C3 candidate sets cannot be compared at R=20.
findings.fix: On the next pod run and save into logs/: `python3 submask_triton.py --verify --roots 3 --plants 32 --rounds 20 | tee logs/triton_verify_r20.log`, `--verify --roots 2 --plants 32`, and `--bench --rounds 20 | tee logs/triton_bench.log` (record `triton.__version__`, torch, GPU). Add a set-level test that exercises all 27 paths: run both implementations at --rounds 19 over the same 2^24 window (about 1,570 hits, no C3) with out_cap raised, and assert the sorted hit-a0 sets are identical.

findings.claim: plant_r20.py prints a wrong expected findability ('(2/e)^3 = 0.40'); the correct probability that a random true root is among k stored roots is E[min(N,k)/N] with N = 1+Poisson(1), i.e. 0.632/0.896/0.976 per lookup, so 0.72 for two roots and 0.93 for three — the memory's '2 roots 40%, 3 roots ~78%' is wrong the same way. The observed 10/16 = 0.625 agrees with 0.72, not 0.40.

summary: Re-derived and re-ran everything in the statistics lens from the saved counters (h100 snapshot + final a100a/a100b status.json), the campaign JSON and the runner logs; script at /tmp/claude-1000/-home-administrator-sha/bc6b4995-3384-44e4-9203-a490e2389533/scratchpad/stats_review.py. (a) The nested-halving decomposition is exactly right: for iid candidates N_{k+1} | N_k ~ Bin(N_k, theta_k) is a Markov chain, so the per-step tests are exactly independent and Bonferroni/Sidak across steps is valid (exact binomial p for the H100 step 25->26, 78->28, is 0.017; x8 = 0.135, x12 = 0.20). All global tests on the pooled counters are null (GLRT deviance over steps 20..28 p = 0.21, Fisher 0.24, all 28 steps p = 0.34). BUT the "aggregate over steps" statistic quoted in the memory file weights step k by n_k, so half its weight sits on the shallowest step and it has almost no power against a deficit at depth, which is the alternative that matters for cost. The depth-weighted statistic (n_28 vs n_0 * 2^-28, exact binomial) pooled over the three pods gives 10 observed vs 16.6 expected, one-sided p = 0.06, 95% CI on the 28-bit pass rate relative to 2^-28 of [0.29, 1.11], i.e. a cost multiplier over the measured 28 bits anywhere in [0.9x, 3.5x]; bits 28-31 are completely unmeasured. The correct statement is "consistent with uniform to 28 bits, a deficit of up to ~3x at 28 bits not excluded, P(C3==0) at full resolution rests on a 4-bit extrapolation plus the zero-hit fleet outcome (95% upper bound 2.9 x 2^-32, no data lower bound)". (b) The Poisson arithmetic all checks: sub/a0 = 9.381e-5 vs theory 9.382e-5; old fleet 1.038 expected, P(no hit) = 0.354, spend about $96; P(hit by 60 h on H100) = 0.879; memorylessness is correct (future hazard unchanged, no swept-context overlap). The new-fleet figure 0.216/h (mean 4.6 h, $22) uses the 9.30e8 a0/s bench rate; the production status files show 8.45e8, 8.25e8 and 7.10e8 a0/s, giving 0.187/h, mean 5.3 h, $25.5 expected, and the cost spread should be quoted (median $18, 90% $59, 95% $76). (c) The audit's 1.79x reproduces exactly as (13783-6541)/4047: it assumes every screened-arm duplicate is a lo-pass and no control duplicate is. Because lo status is a deterministic function of the fixed point (a2,a3), a row can lose at most min(dup,lo) lo-passes, which gives the tightest counts-only bound: deduplicated lift in [2.42x, 3.44x], point estimate 3.405x if duplicates pass at the ordinary rate. The paper's bootstrap CI [2.13,5.82] and sign test (31/9, p = 3.4e-4) reproduce ([2.11,5.83]). The right wording is "3.41x trajectory-counted; hard dedup bound [2.42, 3.44]", not "worst case 1.79x". A rerun of the ~10 duplicate-heaviest screened rows (62% of all duplicates are in one row, t33 c4) with lo gated on fp_seen.add_fp would take ~15 min on one H100 and collapse the interval.

findings.claim: The 'uniform to 28 bits' verdict for C3 rests on an aggregate statistic that has little power against a deficit at depth; the depth-weighted test on the pooled counters shows a 40% deficit at k=28 (p = 0.06 one-sided) and the data cannot bound P(C3==0) at full resolution to better than a factor ~3.

findings.claim: Bonferroni across steps is valid (steps are exactly independent under H0) but it only corrects for choosing the step, not for repeatedly inspecting the counters as they grew; a fixed global statistic evaluated once, or an always-valid sequential test, is the appropriate tool.
findings.evidence: Derivation: for iid candidates, conditional on the N_k elements with low k bits zero, their bit k are independent with P(bit k = 0 | low k bits zero) = theta_k, so N_{k+1} | N_0..N_k ~ Bin(N_k, theta_k) exactly and the (N_k) sequence is Markov; under H0 theta_k = 1/2, so the step z-scores are independent and Bonferroni/Sidak apply. Exact binomial p for the H100 step 25->26 (78 -> 28, z = -2.49 at the snapshot; -2.58 at the earlier 2.31e9-candidate look) is 0.0169; x8 steps (20..27) = 0.135, Sidak 0.127; x12 = 0.20. The 'ratio at k' statistics are nested and correlated, so Bonferroni on them would be wrong. The memory file's step 25->26 was selected after looking at intermediate counters (2.31e9 then 2.96e9 candidates), which no step-wise correction addresses. A Gamma-mixture always-valid p for the depth cell gives no evidence (p ~ 1).
findings.fix: Report the GLRT deviance over the independent steps (chi2 with one dof per step; pooled p = 0.21 for k = 20..27, 0.34 for all 28 steps) as the global test, the depth-weighted binomial as the cost-relevant one-sided test, and evaluate both once on the final counters; do not report a Bonferroni-corrected single step.

findings.claim: The C3 uniformity log's collision line ('distinct values: 67,858 of 68,414') looks like a 1000x collision excess but is an artefact of sampling a0 with replacement; as written it should not be used as a full-resolution check, and the scaling test has the same contamination.

Under uniform independent 32-bit values the expected number of collisions among 68,414 samples is n^2/2^33 = 0.5. c3_scaling.py also draws a0 with replacement (rng.integers), ~2.7e8 per worker-context => ~3% duplicated candidates, which inflates the variance of its deep counts (the '1 vs 2.04 at k=20' cell).

Then the birthday statistic sum(p_i^2) on saved C3 values is the one genuinely 32-bit-resolution test available cheaply (it constrains the second moment of the distribution, not P(C3==0) specifically); on the 3e9 GPU candidates it would be measured to ~1e-4 relative precision if values were streamed to a collision counter.

summary: The table machinery is correct: the GPU multi-root build stores exactly min(r,k) distinct genuine roots per target (the scatter races only decide which root lands in which table, never store a non-root or a duplicate; checked by replicating the exact build logic on 40 random maps with within-step and cross-step collisions), the per-lookup yields E[min(r,k)] = 0.632/0.896/0.977 are right and match the measured 0.2545/0.7244/0.9338 solutions per a0 once the real coverages (0.6337, 0.2644, ~0.0793) are used, and the quantized-table scheme is exact and never wrong (re-run at B=24 on a fresh seed: 664,462/664,462 and 277,025/277,025 stored roots recovered, every recovered value a genuine root, 0 spurious; the 0xFFFFFF sentinel-looking pattern is disambiguated by the completion check, 2430/2430). Three claims need correcting. (1) The planted-preimage found fraction is not (2/e)^3 = 0.40 for two roots or ~0.78 for three: because the true root is size-biased (r* = 1 + Poisson(1)) and is stored with probability min(k,r*)/r*, P(stored) = E[min(r,k)]/E[r] = E[min(r,k)], the same number as the yield, giving 0.72 (two roots) and 0.93 (three). Measured directly on the real tables with 200,000 random u: 0.6348 and 0.8993 (theory 0.6337, 0.8981). The observed 10/16 fits 0.72 (P(X<=10) = 0.28) and is marginally inconsistent with 0.40 (P(X>=10) = 0.06); the 0.40/0.78 figures are P(r* <= k)^3, which ignores the k/r* credit when r* > k. (2) The quantized-table crossover argument uses two wrong constants: an H100 sustains about 1.7e13 int32 ops/s (132 SMs x 64 INT32 lanes x 1.98 GHz), not 6e13, and the Triton kernel already performs about 8e9 random table reads/s on an A100 (9.3e8 a0/s x 8.8 reads per a0), not 1.74e9. With correct numbers B=24 (256 completions per slot, ~22,500 int ops per swept a0) is arithmetic-bound at ~7e8 a0/s on H100 and ~4.3e8 on A100/A6000, i.e. below the memory-bound rate, not '13x below'; a per-slot valid flag (10-byte interleaved record, 40 GiB) cuts that to ~7,300 ops/a0 and restores parity. (3) The kernel keeps the three root tables as separate 16 GB arrays, so each level issues three independent random gathers; per solution, three separate tables need 9.4 gathers against 7.5 for two and 8.0 for one, so on a memory-bound kernel the third root as implemented is a net loss, while interleaving the k roots into one 12- or 16-byte record (48 or 64 GiB, fits an 80 GB card) would need only 3.1 sector visits per solution, up to ~3x fewer DRAM accesses; the quoted 'per LOOKUP 2.13x' for two roots is exactly the interleaved (per-level) count and does not describe the current layout. Nothing found affects correctness of reported preimages, C3 statistics, or the search's memorylessness; the fleet's cost estimate could improve substantially with the interleaved layout, which needs a benchmark on a free pod.

findings.claim: The planted-preimage found fraction for k stored roots is E[min(r,k)]^3, not (2/e)^3 = 0.40 (two roots) or ~0.78 (three roots): 0.72 and 0.93 respectively. plant_r20.py line 81 and the summary carry the wrong expectation.
findings.evidence: Size-biased root count r* = 1 + Poisson(1); the true root is one of r* roots of which min(k,r*) are stored, uniformly with respect to the true root (the stored set is fixed by u-order, the planted W_r is uniform), so P(stored) = E[min(k,r*)/r*] = E[r min(k,r)/r]/E[r] = E[min(r,k)]: 0.6321, 0.8964, 0.9767 (review_tables_a.py). Measured on the real tables with 200,000 random u: P(u in T1) = 0.6348 +/- 0.0011, P(u in T1 or T2) = 0.8993 +/- 0.0007, matching the coverages 0.6337 and 0.8981; cubed 0.256 and 0.727. The observed 10/16 has P(X<=10) = 0.28 under 0.72 but P(X>=10) = 0.06 under 0.40; the Triton verify 8/8 with three roots has probability 0.57 under 0.93. (2/e)^3 and (2.5/e)^3 = 0.778 are P(Poisson(1) <= k-1)^3, the chance the target has at most k roots, which ignores that the true root is still stored with probability k/r* when r* > k.
findings.fix: Change the expectation printed by plant_r20.py to (sum of the k coverages)^3 = 0.72 for two roots, and quote 0.93 for three; the data already agree with it.

findings.claim: The quantized-table throughput argument ('B=24 arithmetic 13x below the H100 memory bottleneck') rests on two wrong constants and its conclusion inverts: at B=24 the completion arithmetic is the bottleneck on H100, A100 and A6000 unless per-slot validity flags are added.
findings.evidence: quantized_table.py lines 88-91 use 6e13 int32 ops/s for an H100 and 1.74e9 lookups/s for the kernel. An H100 SXM issues 64 INT32 ops per SM per clock (CUDA arithmetic-throughput table, cc 9.0): 132 x 64 x 1.98 GHz = 1.67e13; A100 SXM 9.75e12; A6000 (84 SMs, 1.8 GHz) 9.7e12. The Triton kernel with three separate root tables issues 3 + 3c + 3c^2 = 8.80 random 4-byte gathers per a0 (c = 0.9774), so the measured 9.3e8 a0/s on an A100 is 8.2e9 reads/s, not 1.74e9. Each read of a 24-bit slot needs 256 completions x ~10 ops (as the script itself counts), i.e. 2,252 completions and ~22,500 int ops per swept a0 when every slot including empties is completed (an empty slot packs to 0xFFFFFF and must be completed to be recognised): caps of 7.4e8 a0/s (H100), 4.3e8 (A100), 4.3e8 (A6000), all below the memory-bound rate. With a valid bit per slot only the 0.977 filled slots per visit are completed: ~7,300 ops/a0, caps 2.3e9 / 1.3e9 / 1.3e9 a0/s, roughly at parity with memory. B=20 is 16x worse; B=28 is fine but packs to 3.5 bytes.
findings.fix: Correct the two constants in quantized_table.py; if quantization is pursued, use an interleaved record of 3 x 24-bit roots plus flag bits (10 bytes, 40 GiB) so only filled slots are completed, and benchmark before relying on it. Also note the build path: packing via a full 16 GiB int32 table needs 12+12+16+12 GiB transient for the third root, which does not fit a 48 GB card; an index-sliced build is required.

findings.claim: Storing the root tables as three separate 16 GB arrays makes the third root a net loss per memory access, and interleaving the k roots into a single record would cut random DRAM accesses per solution by up to ~3x; the quoted 'per LOOKUP 2.13x' gain for two roots is the interleaved count, not the count for the layout actually implemented.
findings.evidence: submask_triton.py lines 111-135 load from t0_ptr, t1_ptr, t2_ptr at the same index at every level (three independent 32-byte sectors), and gpu_submask.build_tables returns separate tensors. With real coverages, gathers per solution are 8.00 (one root, 2.04 gathers / 0.2545 sol per a0), 7.47 (two, 5.41 / 0.7244) and 9.42 (three, 8.80 / 0.9338); per-level visits per solution are 8.00, 3.73 and 3.14, and 8.00/3.73 = 2.14 is the '2.13x per lookup' figure. A 12-byte interleaved record (48 GiB) straddles a 32 B sector 25% of the time (1.25 sectors per visit); a 16-byte record (64 GiB, fits 80 GB) never does and has room for a fourth root (P(r>=4) = 0.019, yield 0.9957^3 = 0.987, +6%) at no extra traffic. Whether the kernel is bandwidth- or latency-bound on the A100 (8.2e9 gathers/s is 13-26% of HBM2e sector peak) cannot be settled without a GPU; the sector-count reduction is exact, the wall-clock gain needs a --bench with --roots 2 vs 3 and an interleaved variant.
findings.fix: Build one tensor of shape (2^32, 3) or (2^32, 4) int32 with the same scatter logic (index [v, r]) and change the three tl.load calls per level to one 12/16-byte load; benchmark on a free pod (not the running ones). If no time for that, benchmark --roots 2 against --roots 3 with the present layout: the analysis predicts two separate tables are about 20% faster per solution.

findings.claim: GPU build races in the second/third-root scatter are benign: no root is stored twice, no non-root is stored, and exactly min(r,k) distinct roots end up stored per target.
findings.evidence: gpu_submask.build_tables lines 56-72: table r only writes u at v = s0(u)-u (always a root); the mask excludes u already held by every previous, fully built table, so tables are disjoint; within a step two new roots of the same v race and one wins, but the loser is not in any table and is picked up by the next table's pass, so table k is filled iff r >= k. Replicated the exact logic on 20 random maps of size 2^16 with step 2^10 (within- and cross-step collisions), with and without shuffling the within-step order to mimic CUDA's nondeterministic scatter winner: all invariants hold (review_tables_b.py). Consistent with measured second-root coverage 26.44% (P(r>=2) = 26.42%) and three-root yield 0.9338 = (0.6337+0.2644+0.0793)^3. Race-induced loss only appears with a byte-packed scatter (three separate byte writes could interleave two roots into a non-root), which would be caught by the completion check but lose the slot; resolve duplicates before scattering if a packed build is written.

findings.claim: Sentinel collision: u = 0xFFFFFFFF is a genuine root of v = 0x20000000 but is indistinguishable from the -1 miss sentinel in the int32 tables, and both on-disk tables hold the sentinel at that entry; the docstring of build_sigma0_table.py says the GPU build avoids this, which is no longer true for gpu_submask.py (SEN = -1).
findings.evidence: s0(0xFFFFFFFF) - 0xFFFFFFFF = 0x20000000; T1[0x20000000] = T2[0x20000000] = 0xFFFFFFFF (review_tables_a.py). gpu_submask.py line 35 uses SEN = -1, whereas build_sigma0_table.py lines 18-24 state 'The GPU build uses the int32 minimum as its sentinel instead'. Effect: one root of one target in 2^32 is lost (conservative, can only miss a solution); the quantized completion actually recovers it but returns it as MISS by convention. MANIFEST.txt also says the GPU runs build tables 'with the same policies' as the on-disk LARGEST-u table, but the CUDA scatter winner is nondeterministic; policy independence was shown in the paper's E3 so this is a wording nit.
findings.fix: Update the two docstrings/MANIFEST wording; no code change needed.

findings.claim: submask_triton.py copies all root tables to host RAM for the rebuild step (48 GB for three roots), an undocumented pod requirement.
findings.evidence: submask_triton.py lines 281-282: cpu_tbls = [t.cpu() for t in tbls]; rebuild.tbl = cpu_tbls. Hits are rare, so the three int(t[v]) reads per hit could be served from the device tensors instead.

findings.claim: Quantized tables re-verified at B=24 on a fresh random probe: exact and never wrong, including the sentinel-pattern edge case that the original probe did not exercise.
findings.evidence: review_tables_c.py, seed 764046051, 2^20 targets per table: first table 664,462/664,462 stored roots recovered exactly, second table 277,025/277,025, every recovered value satisfies s0(u)-u == target, 0 spurious roots from empty slots (expected 0.02-0.05). Roots whose low 24 bits are 0xFFFFFF (the packed pattern of the sentinel) were recovered 2430/2430 from the sentinel-looking pattern, confirming quant_table.py's note that no side bitmap is needed for correctness (a flag is still useful for speed, see the arithmetic finding). Argument check: the completions enumerate every u with the stored low B bits, so the stored root is always among them and passes; anything else that passes is a genuine additional root of the same target, expected 2^(32-B) x 2^-32 = 6e-8 per lookup at B=24, and could at worst duplicate a root held in another table.

summary: The R=20 pipeline is correct end to end, independently of the kernel. With my own planter (standard eight-register SHA-256 written from the specification, validated against hashlib at 64 rounds and against verify_r19.py at 19 and 20 rounds), 200 planted 20-round preimages in the family satisfying Maj(v,a3,a2)==a3 were swept by gpu_submask.sweep_context over a 4096-wide a0 window: with one root table 54 found / 146 unfindable / 0 failures (27% vs 25.5% predicted), with two tables 145 / 55 / 0 failures (72.5% vs 72.2%); zero spurious hits; every hit re-verified by the independent verifier; Maj-violating plants and 19-round digests produce no hits. The production host-side rebuild() from submask_triton.py scores 151/49/0 on 200 further plants. The counting behind the projection checks out from measured table coverage (0.63287, 0.26429; Poisson 0.63212, 0.26424): predicted solutions per swept a0 0.2535/0.7221/0.9339 for 1/2/3 roots vs claimed 0.2548/0.7235/0.934, measured 0.2545 and 0.7242 on CPU; the Maj rate per solution is 9.99e-5 and 1.03e-4 vs (3/4)^32 = 1.0045e-4 (z = -0.19, +1.48), identical at v=0 and v=all-ones; 402,965 sub per 2^32 a0 predicted at three roots vs 402,792-402,826 on the pods. 'expected preimages = sub * 2^-32' is the right statistic (each C3==0 candidate is deterministically a preimage, no double counting across roots or contexts, and it agrees with the independent per-context count 1 * (3/4)^32 * 0.934 = 9.38e-5); the status files' expected_preimages fields equal sub * 2^-32 exactly. The attack model in the code (digest = IV + compress_R(IV, W) on a raw 16-word block, standard IV, no padding, all 256 bits, feed-forward) matches the paper's Attack-model paragraph, and a 20-round hit on the all-ones digest would be a genuine (first) preimage of the 20-round compression function, not a pseudo-preimage or second preimage. Issues are all minor: the C3 aggregate quoted from the earlier audit (z=-0.63) comes from an earlier snapshot, and on the final H100 counters the same aggregate is z=-2.55 driven entirely by the single step 19->20 (pooled over three pods z=-1.07; material effect on the rate at most a few percent); the 0.216/h fleet rate uses the steady-state 4.7 s per context, while cumulative measured throughput gives 0.19-0.20/h (mean 5.0-5.1 h, ~$24), and 4.6 h is the mean for a hit on either target, whereas the all-ones digest alone (two pods) has a mean of about 7 h with an exponential tail (90th percentile ~2.3x the mean); Zaikin's convention cannot be confirmed from local files (his Table 7 words are not stored; the local PDF is a stub); and the Triton production path no longer records the C3 low-bit counters, so uniformity monitoring has stopped.

findings.claim: The counting behind the projection is right: solutions per swept a0 = E[min(N,k)]^3 with the measured table coverages, the collapsed condition holds at (3/4)^32 per solution independent of v, and 402,970 sub per 2^32 a0 at three roots follows.

Predicted sol/a0: 0.2535 (1 root), 0.7221 (2), 0.9339 (3, third root taken as Poisson 0.0803) vs claimed 0.2548 / 0.7235 / 0.934. Measured on CPU over 5 contexts x 2^23 a0 (v random, 0, 0xFFFFFFFF): sol/a0 0.2545 and 0.7242; sub/sol pooled 9.99e-5 (1 root, z=-0.19) and 1.03e-4 (2 roots, z=+1.48) vs (3/4)^32 = 1.0045e-4. findings.claim: 'expected preimages = sub * 2^-32' is the correct statistic for this search and the status files compute it exactly.
findings.evidence: Every candidate counted in sub that passes C3 is rebuilt and forward-verified, so hits = #{C3==0 among sub}; distinct a0, distinct roots (tables 2 and 3 store u != earlier roots; roots_of dedups) and distinct contexts give distinct messages, so there is no double counting. Independent route: per family context the four 32-bit schedule constraints on a0..a3 leave 2^128 * 2^-128 = 1 expected preimage, of which a fraction (3/4)^32 * 0.934 is findable = 9.38e-5, equal to 402,970 * 2^-32. All five status.json files have expected_preimages == sub * 2^-32 to the printed precision (e.g. a100a 0.1725, H100 0.6896).

findings.claim: The C3 halving aggregate quoted in the context ('2,092 of 4,225, z=-0.63, p=0.53; one low step 25->26 z=-2.58') was computed on an earlier snapshot; on the final H100 counters the same 9-step aggregate is z=-2.55, driven entirely by step 19->20.

Materiality: taken at face value as a one-step effect the rate changes by 0.964, i.e. ~4%; the projection is not at risk. findings.claim: The R=20 attack model in the code matches the paper's Attack-model paragraph; a 20-round hit on the all-ones digest would be a genuine preimage of the 20-round compression function, not a pseudo-preimage, free-start or second preimage.
findings.evidence: submask_family.digest/backward_chain and my own compress() agree on 200 random raw blocks at R=19 and R=20 and with verify_r19.py: digest = IV + state after R rounds in register order (a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h) = (a_{R-1},a_{R-2},a_{R-3},a_{R-4},e_{R-1..R-4}), standard IV, 16 unconstrained words, no padding, all 256 bits matched. paper_r19_final.tex lines 99-119 define exactly this. The IV is not chosen by the attacker (so not pseudo-/free-start); no 20-round preimage of the all-ones digest is known (Zaikin: 19 rounds), so a hit is a first preimage; it is not a preimage of the padded hash.
findings.fix: Phrase any announcement as 'a preimage of the 20-round SHA-256 compression function for the all-ones digest (standard IV, feed-forward kept, no padding)'.

findings.claim: Equivalence with Zaikin's convention (feed-forward kept, all 256 bits, standard IV) cannot be verified from the local files; it rests on the paper's reading of his text.
findings.evidence: paper_r19_final.tex lines 142-144 assert the same model; scratchpad/zaikin2026.pdf is a 3 KB stub with no extractable text; Zaikin's Table 7 preimage words are not present anywhere in the repository or scratchpad (grep). The claim that P7 'differs from the preimage in Zaikin's Table 7' implies his words were seen but they were not recorded.

summary: The Triton kernel in /home/administrator/sha/publish/code/submask_triton.py is a faithful port of gpu_submask.py / submask_family.py: shifts are made logical correctly, the int64 table index is the unsigned value, masked loads use the sentinel as the fill value so dead lanes behave as misses, the cumsum/atomic slot logic is correct and out_cap truncation is clean, chunking covers the full 2^32 range exactly once, the C3 formula equals the reference, and rebuild() enumerates exactly the roots the kernel does (roots_of's dedupe is a no-op because build_tables never stores a root twice across tables). I installed Triton 3.8.0 in the CPU venv and executed the actual kernel under TRITON_INTERPRET=1 against the on-disk 1st/2nd-root tables: 12/12 planted R=19 and R=20 preimages agree with gpu_submask.sweep_context (hit sets, sub counters, verified counts), a 2^17 window across the 0xFFFFFFFF->0 wrap and another across the signed 0x7FFFFFFF->0x80000000 boundary with unaligned chunks both give identical hit sets, and out_cap=3 returns exactly 3 valid hits. The three running Triton pods have distinct seeds and their measured sub-rates (402,897 / 402,939 / 402,851 per 2^32 a0) match the 3-root prediction 402,970. Nothing found that could lose a real hit or report a false one inside the kernel/rebuild path; the residual risks are operational (a hit on a pod is retrieved by single scp attempts before the pod is deleted) and cosmetic (silent drop of unverifiable kernel hits, R=19 out_cap truncation, duplicate-a0 double counting).

findings.claim: A verified 20-round hit on a pod can be lost if the post-hit file fetch fails, because the pod is deleted unconditionally in the finally block and the hit words never reach the local host by any other channel.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/run_r20_pod.py lines 130-150: the poll only runs `tail -n 1 run.log; ls HIT.txt`, and after a hit the last line of run.log is 'DONE' (production() logs '*** VERIFIED', then 'ctx', 'stopping on verified hit', 'DONE'), so the runner log never contains the W words. On found=True the loop breaks, each of run.log/status.json/HIT.txt/stdout.log gets ONE scp attempt (errors ignored), then `api('DELETE', ...)` runs regardless. Transient ssh failures do occur (r20_t1_run.log 15:12:40 '<ssh failed>'). attach_pod.py adds one extra fetch of HIT.txt during the poll but also deletes unconditionally. Probability is low (needs consecutive scp failures right after a hit while ssh worked) but the consequence is losing the campaign result.
findings.fix: Add `cat HIT.txt 2>/dev/null` to the ssh poll command so the words land in the local runner log via ssh stdout, and/or skip the DELETE (log loudly instead) when found=True and the local HIT.txt is missing after the fetches.

findings.claim: production() silently discards a kernel hit that rebuild() cannot verify; the reference logs '!!! candidate failed forward verification', the Triton path logs nothing.
findings.evidence: submask_triton.py lines 360-364: `for a0 in hits: for Wm in rebuild(...)` — a hit a0 for which rebuild returns [] leaves no trace in run.log or status.json. Since rebuild's digest check is strictly stronger than the kernel's Maj+C3 test, any discrepancy (e.g. a future edit to K3p or the constants) would look like 'no hit yet' forever instead of an error.
findings.fix: Log a '!!! kernel hit 0x%08x did not rebuild' line and count it in status.json (e.g. tot['unver']).

findings.claim: At R=19 the production path truncates hits to out_cap=16384 per context although ~403,000 collapsed-condition candidates (each a genuine preimage) are produced per 2^32 swept a0, so tot['ver'] and 'a0 per preimage' would be wrong by ~25x.
findings.evidence: run_context default out_cap=1<<14; keep = hit & (slot+pos < out_cap); nh = min(cnt, out_cap). At R=20 hits per context are ~1e-4 so this never triggers; it only matters if submask_triton.py --run is used at --rounds 19 (the running fleet is R=20).
findings.fix: Raise out_cap for R<20 (e.g. 1<<20) or make run_context grow the buffer when cnt exceeds out_cap.

findings.claim: The same a0 can be recorded more than once by the kernel (one entry per (i,j,kk) root combination that hits), and production() then calls rebuild twice, appending duplicate W to found/HIT.txt and inflating tot['ver'].
findings.evidence: sweep stores A0 once per hitting (i,j,kk) iteration (lines 145-149); production() iterates `for a0 in hits` without dedupe. --verify's `ver == st['ver']` would also spuriously report MISMATCH in that case. Requires two independent root chains for one a0 to both pass all tests (~1e-9 per a0 at R=19, negligible at R=20); no hit is lost.
findings.fix: Dedupe `hits` (np.unique) before rebuilding, or dedupe found by W.

findings.claim: Sentinel collision: a root u = 0xFFFFFFFF (at v = 0x20000000) reads as MISS in the kernel, in roots_of and in every reference; this is symmetric across implementations, so it cannot produce a kernel/rebuild disagreement, and it loses at most one root in 2^32.
findings.evidence: MISS32 = -1 in the kernel; roots_of skips u == M; gpu_submask lookup and submask_family attack_context use the same test. sigma0(0xFFFFFFFF) - 0xFFFFFFFF = 0x20000000.
findings.fix: None needed; document if the table format is ever published.

findings.claim: Three-root nested-loop path was not exercisable in the interpreter (only two on-disk tables exist locally); its correctness rests on the GPU --verify (8/8 planted, 3 roots) plus the production sub-rate matching the 3-root prediction (402.9k vs 402,970; a 2-root pipeline would give ~312k), which together rule out the third-table branch being dead or aliased.
findings.evidence: r20_t1/t2/dev_status.json: sub/contexts = 51,570,863/128, 73,737,856/183, 103,935,473/258. Interpreter runs used sigma0_u_table.npy + sigma0_u_table_root2.npy only.

findings.claim: rebuild() depends on 48 GB of host RAM (three 16 GB CPU copies of the GPU tables) made at startup; on a pod with less host memory the process would be OOM-killed before sweeping (it evidently was not), and this is the largest fixed host cost of the Triton path.

findings.fix: Rebuild could instead gather the handful of roots per hit from the GPU tables (three tiny lookups) and avoid the host copies.

findings.claim: Operational observations, not kernel defects: (a) both t1 and t2 solvers were restarted ~10 min after launch with new seeds (throughput 3.6-4.7e8 -> 8.8e8 a0/s), so the first ~48 contexts are absent from the status.json accounting (0.0045 expected preimages, trivial); (b) stop_watcher.py stops ALL pods on any r20*HIT.txt, so a hit on the random-digest hedge pod would also terminate the two all-ones (Zaikin target) pods.
findings.evidence: r20_t1_run.log 15:02 ctx 21 then 15:07 ctx 3; r20_t2_run.log 15:06:50 new 'TRITON ... seed=1138247750' header; stop_watcher.py globs r20*HIT.txt without regard to target.

summary: The pipeline itself holds up: the Triton kernel, the multi-root tables, the planted-preimage test and the C3 statistics are consistent with each other and with theory, and I re-checked two things the project had not: (i) all four "random" R=20 targets reproduce from the recorded seeds (so a preimage of each is known by construction), and (ii) on the all-ones target itself, at R=20, the collapsed-condition rate is 1.0081e-4 (predicted 1.0045e-4) and C3 is uniform on its low 4-12 bits over 55,090 candidates from 2^31 swept a0 (scratchpad/c3_ones_check.py, .log), so nothing measured depends on the target. What is not yet in order is the write-up layer: (1) an ops flaw -- a hit on the hedge (random-target) pod fires the global stop and kills both all-ones pods; (2) the frozen companion paper's "2^64 per context-equivalent / no context choice removes the obstruction / 2^71.4 total work" and the R19 paper's "does not reach 20 rounds" and "two GPU-hours per digest" are superseded by the project's own family and must be reconciled explicitly (the 2^32 C3 factor survives; the 2^23 base reduction is what changed); (3) provenance gaps in the current fleet (both all-ones solvers were restarted with new seeds at 15:06-15:07, the third pod's solver was started by hand on the reused a100a pod, the MANIFEST hashes are stale); (4) cost must be quoted in explicit units (2^45.4 swept a0 with 3 roots = 2^47.3 with 1 root ~ 2^48.5 lookups ~ 14 A100-hours; cold start negligible at R=20 but dominant at R=19); (5) wording: a 20-round all-ones hit is a first preimage (not a second preimage -- that phrase is only right at 19 rounds), the random-message targets are second preimages in the formal sense and should be labelled, and "first" must be qualified as "first practically computed" given the 43/45-step theoretical attacks. Zaikin's exact statement about 20 rounds could not be verified locally (only the abstract is available here) and must be quoted verbatim from the full text.

findings.claim: A hit on the hedge pod (random target d962ca30..., pod 'dev') will stop the two all-ones pods, aborting the headline search with probability about 1/3.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/stop_watcher.py globs r20*HIT.txt (any tag) and touches r20_GLOBAL_STOP; run_r20_pod.py lines 135-136 and attach_pod.py lines 71-72 break and delete their pod on GLOBAL_STOP. attach_pod.py fetches r20_dev_HIT.txt immediately on a hit (line 70). Rates are equal per pod (0.0718/h each, 4.7 s per 2^32 context), so P(first hit is the hedge) = 1/3.
findings.fix: Make the stop target-specific (write the target hex into the HIT file name or into GLOBAL_STOP and have each runner compare against its own --hash), or exclude the dev tag from stop_watcher's glob. If a hedge hit does fire first, relaunch the all-ones pair immediately and say so in the write-up (search is memoryless, only ~1 min of table build is lost).

findings.claim: The frozen companion paper's central quantitative claims are superseded by the project's own result and the write-up must reconcile them, not silently replace them.
findings.evidence: paper_r20_barrier.tex lines 77-78 ('The obstruction is Sigma0(a4) subtracted directly inside W9, which no context choice removes'), 83-84 ('2^64 per context-equivalent'), 761-763 ('R=20 is not solved... 2^71.4 expected total work'); paper_r19_final.tex lines 1165-1172 ('The same construction does not reach 20 rounds'). The family gives 2^45.4 swept a0 (3 roots) / 2^47.3 (1 root) per R=20 preimage; the fleet expects a hit in ~7 h on two A100s. The companion's own section 'A Context Family that Removes a2 from C0' (lines 361-381) records e8=0xFFFFFFFF and a4=a3 and dismisses it.
findings.fix: Proposed text for the new write-up: 'The companion note bounded this attack family at 2^64 per context-equivalent, i.e. 2^32 times the 19-round per-context cost, and located the obstruction in Sigma0(a4) inside W9. The factor 2^32 stands: the fourth constraint C3 is paid in full as a filter, and its residual is uniform to 24 bits on random targets and to 12-16 bits on the all-ones target. What changed is the base. The context family a4=a5=v, e8=e9=0xFFFFFFFF removes the fixed-point iteration (2^15) and collapses the W9 consistency check to the bitwise condition Maj(v,a3,a2)=a3 (2^8.7), lowering the 19-round cost from 2^38.3 to 2^15.3 swept a0 and hence the 20-round cost from 2^70 to 2^47. The note's statement that no context choice removes the obstruction was wrong in the form stated: the context choice does not remove Sigma0(a4) but makes the a2,a3-dependence of W9 borrow-free, which is what the heavy-cycle argument assumed could not happen. The note's own section on the e8 = 0xFFFFFFFF family used a4=a3, tying a context word to an unknown; tying a4 to a5 instead costs nothing per candidate.' State this in the abstract of the new paper and in an erratum paragraph for the companion.

Quantized tables can be rescued without a validity flag: since the low B bits and the completion bits occupy disjoint positions, u = lo ^ (i<<B) exactly and sigma0 is GF(2)-linear, so sigma0(u) = sigma0(lo) ^ sigma0(i<<B) with sigma0(i<<B) a 256-entry constant table; the completion check becomes ~4 int ops (xor, add, sub, compare) instead of ~10, giving ~9k ops per swept a0 and a cap of ~1.8e9 a0/s on H100 (parity with memory), ~1.1e9 on A100.
